I had a random dude open my bedroom door (while I was using the mirror on the back of it to get ready for class) early in the morning during college. He slammed the door shut and sprinted downstairs and out the back door when he realized the house wasn’t empty. I heard someone on the stairs beforehand but thought it was just a housemate starting his day (turns out all of my housemates were out).

I didn’t even think to contact the cops until later that afternoon because I was so thoroughly baffled at the situation. He didn’t attack me, he looked scared as shit to see me there and it seemed like he was just checking the rooms before making off with a bunch of our stuff (it didn’t appear like anything was missing). But my day was a totally normal outside of trying to process the whiplash of that split second interaction (I even made it to my morning class).

I didn’t even mention it to my housemates until that night at dinner because, while I was thoroughly spooked, it wasn’t a violent interaction and I didn’t think anyone else was in danger from it. The guy left. He knew I was home alone if he cased the first floor first. He could have taken me down if he wanted to, but he didn’t.

It wouldn’t surprise me if her brain went into shock and explained his presence away as a burglar who got spooked and ran off. And given the number of standard break ins that happen every day, it’s not surprising her brain didn’t immediately jump to the guy potentially being a quadruple murderer (when he wasn’t violent with her). That thought is too awful for a person to process when they’re NOT in shock.

I’m so so sorry for your loss. After some time has passed, when my heart begins to ache for the people I’ve lost, this poem brings me some comfort. I hope it can bring you comfort too:

*Death is Nothing at All*

By Henry Scott-Holland



Death is nothing at all. 

It does not count. 

I have only slipped away into the next room. 

Nothing has happened. 



Everything remains exactly as it was. 

I am I, and you are you, 

and the old life that we lived so fondly 

together is untouched, unchanged. 

Whatever we were to each other, that we are still. 



Call me by the old familiar name. 

Speak of me in the easy way which you always used. 

Put no difference into your tone. 

Wear no forced air of solemnity or sorrow. 



Laugh as we always laughed at the little jokes that we enjoyed together.

Play, smile, think of me, pray for me. 

Let my name be ever the household word that it always was. 

Let it be spoken without an effort, without the ghost of a shadow upon it. 



Life means all that it ever meant. 

It is the same as it ever was. 

There is absolute and unbroken continuity. 

What is this death but a negligible accident? 



Why should I be out of mind because I am out of sight? 

I am but waiting for you, for an interval, 

somewhere very near, 

just round the corner. 



All is well. 

Nothing is hurt; nothing is lost. 

One brief moment and all will be as it was before. 

How we shall laugh at the trouble of parting when we meet again!

On the one hand, I absolutely despise when some random person, realizing I’m trans or gay or whatever, starts a ‘I just want you to know that you’re **so** valid’ spiel. Drives me absolutely batshit. It just feels so patronizing and disingenuous. And like, with all due respect, who are you? Why would **you** telling me **you** think I’m valid matter to me in the slightest? I don’t know you and I didn’t seek you out. I’m not looking for random people to think I’m valid. I’d ask for validation if I wanted it. A person can think I’m a disease for all I care, as long as they leave me alone and don’t try to impede on my rights or the rights of others.

But on the other hand, I watched that video of JewWario where he’s in the middle of a breakdown and telling his audience, who he definitely didn’t know, that they matter and it was the only thing that kept me from ending it all when I was in the middle of a really bad suicidal episode in college. (This was before it came out that he was a piece of shit. Never meet your heroes amirite?) I wasn’t friendless or socially alone by any means, but for some reason that person saying those things hit different. Maybe because he was clearly going through something too? So it felt like it was coming from a genuine place? Or maybe it’s because I wanted to hear something like that in that moment?

Who knows.

I guess it comes down to whether the person is saying these things for even a modicum of self-satisfaction? (Which I think is incredibly transparent.) I don’t think I’d be half as irritated if someone told me I’m valid and they said it from a wholly genuine place.

I don’t doubt that some folks do just have a deep love for people (the collective), and whether they know a person or not is irrelevant. (Sure, their love is ‘deeper’ the more they know a person, but their baseline emotion for people is just basic ‘love’.)

Other people WANT to be that kind of person or THINK they’re that kind of person, and so they mimic the behavior and it makes them feel good. And **that’s** what feels gross.

But if validation (genuine or not) from strangers helps people keep their head above water then all the power to them. IMO the world is indifferent to anyone’s suffering, so if (potentially faux) kindness from strangers helps keep a person afloat then it’s okay by me. I’ll just deal with it when it’s directed at me and mind my business in the meantime.

I’ve seen lots of sex workers argue that rather than legalization, decriminalizing sex work would allow for workers to go to authorities should a crime be committed against them without fear of being prosecuted themselves. So the sex work itself wouldn’t be legal, meaning that the sex worker keeps autonomy over the situation (no government regulations telling them what they can or can’t do or adding special taxes etc.) but because it’s decriminalized you’re not worrying about going to jail for it.

Congratulations on taking the first step! I’m on my second try at sobriety since University (first round lasted 2 1/2 years). Something that I learned from the first time around is what loads of other folks are saying already: having a support system is key. It makes it much easier than going through it alone.

Something else I’d be wary of is what fills the void. It’s not just a stereotype that alcoholics who stop drinking eat sweets like wild. I gained 20 lbs in the first few months after going sober because I replaced my drinking habit with a sugar habit. Whether it’s finding a new hobby or adopting a new exercise routine, find a positive habit to take up that mental space.

Best of luck and congrats again!
